title: Spark Connect and Deployment Modes

concepts.heading: How Spark Connect Splits Client and Server
concepts.body: Spark Connect, introduced in Spark 3.4, is a decoupled client-server architecture. The client is a thin library that can live in an application server, an IDE or a notebook. It translates DataFrame operations into unresolved logical plans, encodes them with protocol buffers and sends them over gRPC to the Spark Connect endpoint on the server. The endpoint turns them into Spark logical plan operators, and from there the normal optimizer and execution run, so every Spark optimization still applies. Results stream back through gRPC as Apache Arrow-encoded row batches. Because only plans travel, the server never needs the client's Python process. A client only needs the lightweight package, for example `pip install pyspark-client`. To use it, set the `SPARK_REMOTE` environment variable, start the shell with `bin/pyspark --remote "sc://localhost"`, or build a session in code with `SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://localhost").getOrCreate()`. The default server port is 15002. Without one of these mechanisms the session works as before, without Spark Connect.

concepts.heading: What Changes for the Developer
concepts.body: Because the client does not run inside the driver process, some classic habits stop working. In PySpark the client does not use Py4J, so private fields that hold the JVM objects, such as `df._jdf`, cannot be accessed. The protocol describes declarative logical plans, so it does not support all execution APIs, most importantly RDDs. The client is session based, so it has no access to the static Spark configuration or the SparkContext, and an administrator must change settings such as `spark.executor.memory` on the server. Most DataFrame, function and Column APIs work, and most streaming APIs are supported. The gains are operational. Stability: an application that uses too much memory only affects its own process, not a shared driver. Upgradability: the server can be upgraded independently while applications keep working, as long as the RPC definitions stay backward compatible. Debuggability: you can debug from an IDE. Spark Connect has no built-in authentication, so it is placed behind an authenticating proxy.

concepts.heading: Client Mode and Cluster Mode
concepts.body: The deploy mode says where the driver process runs. In client mode the submitter launches the driver, directly inside the `spark-submit` process, and the input and output of the application are attached to the console. This fits interactive work such as the `pyspark` shell and is also the right choice when you submit from a gateway machine next to the workers. In cluster mode the framework launches the driver inside the cluster, so the driver sits on a worker node. Because the driver schedules tasks and must be reachable by its executors, it should run close to them, which is why cluster mode is common when you submit from a machine far from the workers, such as a laptop. The default of `--deploy-mode` is `client`, so `spark-submit --master yarn app.py` runs the driver on the submitting node. Standalone mode does not support cluster mode for Python applications, so a `.py` file cannot be submitted that way; use client mode or another cluster manager. With standalone cluster mode, `--supervise` restarts a driver that exits with a non-zero code.

concepts.heading: Master URLs and Cluster Managers
concepts.body: The `--master` option tells Spark where to run. A cluster manager is the external service that acquires executors, and Spark supports three: its own standalone manager, Hadoop YARN and Kubernetes. The master URL selects among them: `spark://HOST:7077` for standalone (7077 is the default port), `yarn` for YARN, whose cluster location comes from `HADOOP_CONF_DIR`, and `k8s://HOST:PORT` for Kubernetes. For yarn and k8s the `--deploy-mode` value decides client or cluster. Local mode needs no cluster at all: `local` runs with one worker thread and no parallelism, `local[K]` uses K threads, and `local[*]` uses as many threads as logical cores. It suits tests and learning on one machine. Each application gets its own executor processes that live for the whole application, which isolates applications, but data cannot be shared between two applications without an external store. For Python dependencies, `--py-files` distributes `.py`, `.zip` and `.egg` files together with the application.

examPoints: Spark Connect sends unresolved logical plans as protocol buffers over gRPC and streams back Arrow-encoded batches; the client has no Py4J, no `_jdf`, no RDD or SparkContext and no static configuration.

Default deploy mode is client (driver inside the spark-submit process, console attached); use cluster mode when submitting from a far or closable machine; standalone does not run Python applications in cluster mode.
Cluster managers are standalone, YARN and Kubernetes; master URLs are local, local[K], local[*], spark://HOST:PORT, yarn and k8s://HOST:PORT.

quiz.q: A developer sets `export SPARK_REMOTE="sc://localhost"` and starts `./bin/pyspark` with no code change. What does `type(spark)` show?
choices: `pyspark.sql.session.SparkSession`, because the variable only affects the executors
`pyspark.sql.streaming.StreamingSession`, because remote sessions are for streams
`pyspark.sql.connect.session.SparkSession`, a Spark Connect client session
`pyspark.sql.context.SQLContext`, because remote shells use the legacy entry point
quiz.explain: With SPARK_REMOTE set, the new session is a Spark Connect session, and its type contains `.connect.`. The variable changes the client, not the executors, and no code change is needed. Streaming sessions and SQLContext are not entry points that Spark Connect introduces.

quiz.q: A team submits a long job to a Spark standalone cluster with `--deploy-mode cluster` and wants the driver restarted automatically if it exits with a non-zero code. Which option provides that?
choices: `--supervise`, which restarts the driver in standalone cluster mode
`--py-files`, which restarts the driver when the archive changes
`--master local[*]`, which keeps the driver inside the same process
`--packages`, which re-resolves the dependencies and relaunches the driver
quiz.explain: `--supervise` is the option for standalone cluster mode that makes sure the driver is restarted when it fails with a non-zero exit code. `--py-files` only distributes Python files, `local[*]` selects local mode, and `--packages` resolves Maven coordinates.

recap: Spark Connect is a thin client sending unresolved plans over gRPC with Arrow results, and it gives up RDDs, SparkContext and static configuration. Deploy mode decides where the driver runs: client by default, cluster inside the cluster.

title: Pandas API on Spark and Pandas UDFs

concepts.heading: Why Use the Pandas API on Spark
concepts.body: The pandas API on Spark gives pandas users a familiar API whose operations run distributed on Spark, so a script no longer has to fit on one machine. You import it with `import pyspark.pandas as ps` and write code such as `psdf = ps.DataFrame({'id': range(10)})`. It is lazy like Spark, and all Spark features, such as the web UI, the history server and the deployment modes, work as they do for other jobs. It does not aim at 100 percent pandas compatibility, and the Spark documentation recommends PySpark for people who are new to Spark. Conversions matter. `sdf.pandas_api()` turns a Spark DataFrame into a distributed pandas-on-Spark DataFrame, and `psdf.to_spark()` goes back. In contrast, `psdf.to_pandas()` and `sdf.toPandas()` collect every row to the driver, so use them only on small data. Because execution is lazy, `psdf.spark.explain()` prints the Spark plan before anything runs, and an `Exchange` node marks a shuffle. `DataFrame.spark.checkpoint()` cuts a huge plan that has become slow to plan.

concepts.heading: Index, Shuffles and Single-Partition Traps
concepts.body: Most performance questions here come from the index. When a Spark DataFrame is converted, a default index is attached, and `compute.default_index_type` chooses how. `sequence` uses a window with no partition specification, so the data can end up in a single partition on one node and should be avoided for large data. `distributed-sequence` is the default and builds a globally sequential index in a distributed way. `distributed` uses monotonically increasing ids, which are not consecutive but almost free. Best practice: pass an index column when converting, for example `sdf.pandas_api(index_col='id')`, and use `distributed` or `distributed-sequence` for large data. Operations on two different DataFrames are disallowed by default because they need a join; `compute.ops_on_diff_frames` enables them. Some calls shuffle by nature, such as `sort_values`. `DataFrame.rank` uses a window without partitions and moves everything to one partition (`Exchange SinglePartition`), so prefer `GroupBy.rank`. Avoid column names that start and end with `__`, and duplicated column names.

concepts.heading: Pandas UDFs and Their Types
concepts.body: A pandas UDF is a user-defined function that Spark runs with Arrow to move data and pandas to work on it. It is vectorized: the function receives batches of values as a `pd.Series` instead of one row at a time, which is why it is usually faster than a row-at-a-time Python UDF. You define it with `pandas_udf` and Python type hints, for example `@pandas_udf('double')` above `def plus_one(s: pd.Series) -> pd.Series: return s + 1`. Series to Series: the output must have the same length as the input. Iterator of Series to Iterator of Series: same length overall, useful when an expensive state, such as a loaded model, is initialized once. Iterator of a tuple of Series covers multiple columns. Series to Scalar behaves like an aggregate: it reduces a Series to one value and works in `groupBy().agg()` and in unbounded windows. It does not support partial aggregation, and all data for a group or window is loaded into memory. Type hints use `pandas.Series`, or `pandas.DataFrame` for struct columns. The older `PandasUDFType` style is discouraged and will be deprecated.

concepts.heading: Pandas Function APIs: applyInPandas and mapInPandas
concepts.body: Pandas function APIs apply a Python function to a whole DataFrame instead of a Column, so they are called on the DataFrame and not inside `select`. `groupBy('k').applyInPandas(fn, schema)` is split-apply-combine: the function takes one `pandas.DataFrame` that holds all rows of a group and returns another one, and you must give the output schema. All data of a group is loaded into memory before the function runs, and the `maxRecordsPerBatch` limit is not applied to groups, so one skewed group can cause an out-of-memory error. `df.mapInPandas(fn, schema)` has no grouping: the function takes an iterator of `pandas.DataFrame` batches and yields DataFrames, and the output can have any length, so it can filter rows or expand them. A Series to Series pandas UDF cannot do this because its output length must match its input. Quick selector: one value per row, use a Series to Series UDF; one value per group inside `agg`, use a Series to Scalar UDF; arbitrary pandas logic per group, use `applyInPandas`; arbitrary logic per batch, use `mapInPandas`.

examPoints: Pandas API on Spark: `import pyspark.pandas as ps`, distributed and lazy, Spark UI and deploy modes unchanged; `pandas_api()` stays distributed while `toPandas()` and `to_pandas()` collect to the driver.
Default index type is distributed-sequence; `sequence` and `DataFrame.rank` pull data into one partition; check plans with `psdf.spark.explain()` and look for Exchange.

Series to Series must keep the length, Series to Scalar aggregates, applyInPandas loads a whole group in memory, mapInPandas returns any number of rows; pandas UDFs are faster because they use Arrow batches.

quiz.q: A large pandas-on-Spark job builds its default index with `compute.default_index_type` set to `sequence` and slows down. Which setting keeps a globally sequential index but builds it in a distributed way?
choices: `distributed`, because it gives consecutive numbers without any shuffle
`monotonic`, because it numbers rows in the order of the input files
`local-sequence`, because it numbers rows inside each executor first
`distributed-sequence`, which is also the default index type
quiz.explain: `sequence` runs a window without partitions and can put all data on one node. `distributed-sequence` still produces a globally sequential index but computes it across the cluster. `distributed` is cheap but its values are not consecutive, and the other two names are not index types.

quiz.q: A grouped aggregate pandas UDF (Series to Scalar) is used in `groupBy().agg()` on a very large group. Which statement describes its behavior?
choices: It aggregates partially on each executor first, so memory is never an issue
It loads all data of a group or window into memory, with no partial aggregation
It returns one value per input row, so the group is never held in memory
It splits each group into batches of `maxRecordsPerBatch` rows to protect memory
quiz.explain: A Series to Scalar pandas UDF does not support partial aggregation, and all data for a group or window is loaded into memory, which is a risk for skewed groups. It reduces a Series to one value, not one value per row, and the batch size limit does not apply to groups.

recap: Pandas API on Spark keeps pandas syntax but runs distributed and lazy, so mind the index, single-partition operations and conversions to the driver. Pandas UDFs use Arrow batches; length rules and group memory decide which type fits.

title: Final Review: Decision Cheat-Sheet Across the Seven Domains

concepts.heading: Domains 1 and 2: Architecture and Spark SQL (20 and 20 percent)
concepts.body: Architecture: the driver plans and schedules, executors run tasks and hold cached data, and a job is split into stages at shuffle boundaries and stages into tasks. Transformations are lazy and actions such as `count`, `collect` or `write` trigger a job. `cache()` uses the storage level MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER by default. A shuffle moves data between partitions and is the expensive step. `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` is 200, but Adaptive Query Execution, on by default since 3.2, coalesces small shuffle partitions at run time. Modules: Spark SQL and DataFrames, Structured Streaming, pandas API on Spark, and `pyspark.mllib`, which is in maintenance mode. Spark SQL: reading and writing JDBC and files; SQL can query files directly; the default save mode is `errorifexists`, with append, overwrite and ignore as alternatives. Tables can be saved with partitioning, bucketing and sorting. A temporary view lives in one session, a global temporary view lives in the `global_temp` database and is shared by sessions of the application.

concepts.heading: Domains 3 and 4: DataFrame API and Tuning (30 and 10 percent)
concepts.body: Domain 3 is the heaviest, so most points come from reading code. Know column and row operations, `dropDuplicates`, aggregations such as `approx_count_distinct`, date and epoch functions, joins, unions and schemas on read and write. Spark 4 enables ANSI mode by default, so invalid casts and parses can raise errors; `try_*` functions return null instead. A cross join needs no special setting, because `spark.sql.crossJoin.enabled` has been true since 3.0. A broadcast join sends a small table to every executor and avoids a shuffle of the large one. Built-in functions beat Python UDFs because the optimizer understands them. A broadcast variable ships read-only data once to each executor; an accumulator only adds, and its updates are applied exactly once only when made inside actions; inside transformations a re-executed task can add twice. Tuning: `repartition` shuffles into more or fewer partitions, `coalesce` only reduces without a full shuffle, and AQE also handles skewed joins. A task is retried up to `spark.task.maxFailures`, default 4. For out-of-memory errors read the driver and executor logs: `collect` on big data hurts the driver, skew hurts one executor.

concepts.heading: Domains 5, 6 and 7: Streaming, Spark Connect and pandas (10, 5 and 5 percent)
concepts.body: Structured Streaming treats a stream as an unbounded table and runs micro-batches by default. A checkpoint location stores progress and state for fault tolerance, and exactly-once results need a replayable source and an idempotent sink. Output modes are append, update and complete. Event-time windows with a watermark let state be dropped; `dropDuplicates` stores all past records as state without a watermark, while with a watermark on an event-time column old state is dropped, and `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark` (3.5) deduplicates within the watermark delay. Trigger once is deprecated, so use `availableNow`; the continuous trigger is experimental. Stateful processing with Python uses `applyInPandasWithState` (3.4) or `transformWithStateInPandas` (4.0.0), while `mapGroupsWithState` is legacy. Spark Connect (3.4) is a thin client that sends plans over gRPC and has no RDDs, SparkContext or Py4J. Default deploy mode is client, and standalone has no cluster mode for Python applications. Pandas API on Spark is distributed pandas; `toPandas` collects to the driver. A pandas UDF uses Arrow batches, and Series to Series keeps the length.

concepts.heading: Weights, Time and Answering Strategy
concepts.body: The exam has 45 scored questions, plus up to 10 unscored ones, in 90 minutes, which is about two minutes per scored question. All are multiple choice, and the pass mark is not published, so aim high. The weights are: Architecture and Components 20, Spark SQL 20, DataFrame API Applications 30, Troubleshooting and Tuning 10, Structured Streaming 10, Spark Connect 5 and Pandas API on Spark 5 percent. Out of 45 questions that is roughly 9, 9, 13 to 14, 4 to 5, 4 to 5, 2 and 2 questions. So study order is domain 3, then 1 and 2, then 4 and 5, then 6 and 7, and domains 1 to 3 together carry 70 percent. Read each code snippet line by line and predict the output before looking at the choices. Check for lazy evaluation traps (no action, no work), the version a feature needs, and the word that decides the question, such as only, default, driver or after the watermark. Drop choices built on deprecated or removed APIs.

examPoints: Weights: D1 Architecture 20, D2 Spark SQL 20, D3 DataFrame API 30, D4 Troubleshooting and Tuning 10, D5 Structured Streaming 10, D6 Spark Connect 5, D7 Pandas API on Spark 5 percent of 45 scored questions in 90 minutes.

Defaults to recall: ANSI mode on in Spark 4, crossJoin enabled, cache level MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER, maxFailures 4, shuffle partitions 200 with AQE coalescing, deploy mode client, save mode errorifexists.

Version and status facts: availableNow replaces Trigger once, continuous trigger is experimental, dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark 3.5, Spark Connect 3.4, mapGroupsWithState is legacy, mllib is in maintenance mode.

quiz.q: Spark Connect and the pandas API on Spark carry 5 percent each. Of the 45 scored questions, about how many belong to those two domains together?
choices: About 4 to 5 questions, because together they carry 10 percent
About 9 questions, because each of them carries around 20 percent of the exam
About 14 questions, because that is the share of the DataFrame API domain
About 2 questions, because they are tested only as one shared small section
quiz.explain: 5 plus 5 is 10 percent, and 10 percent of 45 is 4.5, so about 4 to 5 questions. Nine questions is the size of a 20 percent domain, 13 to 14 is the 30 percent DataFrame API domain, and each of the two small domains alone already accounts for about 2.

quiz.q: A team still runs a one-off backfill with `Trigger.once` in a Structured Streaming job. Which trigger replaces it?
choices: `continuous`, which is the supported default for backfills
`processingTime`, set to zero seconds for a single batch
`microBatch`, which processes the available data once and stops
`availableNow`, which runs the available data and stops
quiz.explain: Trigger once is deprecated and `availableNow` replaces it: it processes everything available, possibly in several batches, and then stops. The continuous trigger is experimental, and a processing-time trigger keeps running on an interval. `microBatch` is not a trigger name.

recap: Spend time by weight: DataFrame API first, then architecture and SQL, then tuning and streaming, then Connect and pandas. Recall the defaults and the version facts, read code line by line and remember that lazy evaluation needs an action.
